items.label: text
items.text: To be 100% correct 'molar mass' and 'mass of 1 mole' are not exactly the same thing and have different units: molar mass has units of g/mol and the mass of 1 mole has units of g. items.label: section_header
items.text: HINT

items.label: text
items.text: Don't get too reliant on learning formulae for doing simple calculations. If 1 mole weighs 100g, it should be fairly obvious to you that 2 moles will weigh twice as much, 10 moles will weigh 10 times as much and 0.2 moles will weigh 0.2 times as much.

items.label: section_header
items.text: HINT HINT

items.label: text
items.text: If 1 mol weighs 18 g, then you need to find out how many times 18 goes into 54 to find out how many moles you have. On the other hand, if you feel safer using a formula, use it. items.label: section_header
items.text: SIMPLE CALCULATIONS WITH MOLES

items.label: text
items.text: You need to be able to interconvert between a mass in grams and an amount in moles for a given substance. There is a simple formula that you can learn:

items.label: formula
items.text: n u m b e r o f m o l e = \frac { \ m a s s \left ( g \right ) } { \ m a s s \left ( 1 \ m o l e \left ( g \right ) \right ) }

items.label: text
items.text: You can rearrange this formula to find whatever you want. If rearranging this expression causes you problems, you can learn a simple triangular arrangement to help you.

items.label: section_header
items.text: Finding the mass of 0.2 mol of calcium carbonate, CaCO3

items.label: text
items.text: Relative atomic masses: C = 12, O = 16, Ca = 40.

items.label: text
items.text: First find the relative formula mass of calcium carbonate.

items.label: text
items.text: 1 mol of CaCO₃has a mass of 100g.

items.label: formula
items.text: M \, { \mathbf s } \left ( g \right ) & = \text {number of m oles } \times \text {mass of 1 mole } \left ( g \right ) \\ & = 0 . 2 \times 1 0 0 \\ & = 2 0 g

items.label: text
items.text: 0.2 mol of CaCO₃ has a mass of 20 g.

items.text: Finding the number of moles in 54 g of water,H2O

items.label: text
items.text: Relative atomic masses: H = 1, O = 16.

items.label: text
items.text: 1 mol of H2O has a mass of 18g.

items.label: formula
items.text: 1 m o l \, o f \, H _ { 2 } O \, h a s \, a \, m a s s \, o f \, 1 8 g , \\ N u m b e r \, o f \, m o l \, e = \frac { \ m a s \, ( g ) } { \ m a s s \, o f \, 1 \, m o l \, ( g ) } \\ = \frac { 5 4 } { 1 8 } \\ = 3 m o l \\ 5 4 \, o f \, water \, i s \, 3 m o l

items.label: text
items.text: 54 g of water is 3 mol.
